issues.legal_issue: A state law acquiring an electricity undertaking is not repugnant to central electricity legislation when the central provisions for purchasing undertakings do not apply to the acquired company and the laws operate in different fields.
material_facts: The state enacted a law to acquire an undertaking involved in completing a hydroelectric project, citing delay, public interest, and an acute power shortage.
The company was not a licensee under the electricity legislation governing supply and use of electrical energy.
The central law’s provisions for purchasing undertakings applied to licensees, and the provisions made applicable to generating companies did not include those purchase provisions.
The state law provided for acquisition of the undertaking and compensation; the central laws made general provision for the supply and use of electrical energy.
issues.conclusion: The state law did not conflict or create repugnancy with the central electricity laws, and presidential assent was therefore unnecessary. The constitutional challenge failed and the appeals were dismissed. The Court did not decide whether the state law fell under the State List entry on water and water power or the Concurrent List entry on electricity.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 245, 246 and 254 of the Constitution allocate legislative powers and govern repugnancy between state and central laws. Repugnancy requires actual inconsistency, occupation of the same field, or an intention by Parliament to enact an exhaustive code; a mere possibility of conflict is insufficient, and courts should, where possible, reconcile the laws. The Court relied on Shyamakant Lal v. Rambhajan Singh, Deepchand v. State of U.P., Tika Ramji v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Zaverbhai Amaidas v. State of Bombay, and M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India. It considered the Indian Electricity Act, 1910, including sections 6 and 7A, and the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948, including sections 2(4A), 2(6), 26A and 37. The purchase provisions in the 1910 Act applied to licensees, while the provisions made applicable to generating companies did not include those provisions. As the company was not a licensee and the state law and central laws operated in different fields, there was no repugnancy. The Court left unresolved whether the state law was referable to the State List entry on water and water power or the Concurrent List entry on electricity.

predicates.constitutional_validity_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging the constitutional validity of a law.
predicates.state_law_acquires_electricity_undertaki: The challenged state law acquires an electricity undertaking.
predicates.company_not_covered_by_central_purchase_: The company whose undertaking is acquired does not fall within the class of persons to whom the central law’s provisions for purchasing undertakings apply.
predicates.state_and_central_laws_operate_in_differ: The state law addresses acquisition and compensation, while the central laws address the supply and use of electrical energy.

issues.definition: When a constitutional-validity appeal concerns a state law acquiring an electricity undertaking, and the company is outside the central purchase provisions while the laws operate in different fields, the state acquisition law is not repugnant to central law.
